implementation_notes: In C the poltergeist is a `struct` that exists only to group a call site, or a struct whose only purpose is to be filled in and passed to one function. The C-specific complication is that the object model is optional: the honest translation of most poltergeists into C is simply to delete the struct and call the function, and the only thing keeping the struct alive is symmetry with another codebase. Diagnosis is `grep -n '<name>' *.c *.h` and reading the construction sites; if no pointer to the struct is ever stored anywhere, it is a poltergeist.
idiom_name: one-shot struct in a header with no API of its own
pitfalls: A struct used as a named parameter bundle (even if passed once) is closer to a parameter object than a poltergeist; the distinction is whether the bundle accumulates.
A `struct` forward-declared in a header and defined in one .c file can look like a helper while actually being an opaque handle — that is the opposite of a poltergeist.
Static initialisers of poltergeist structs in headers produce one instance shared across translation units, which is a different bug with the same shape.
